steps.title: Short-lived access token
steps.caption: The app calls the API with a 10-minute access token. Once it expires, the API answers 401.
steps.body: After sign-in the app holds two tokens: an **access token** that lives for minutes (10 here) and a **refresh token**, RT1, the first of a new **token family** on the authorization server. API calls carry only the access token; the refresh token is never sent to the API. When the access token has expired, the API answers `401` with `error="invalid_token"`, and that is the app's cue to refresh.

steps.title: Refresh and rotate
steps.caption: The app sends RT1 to the token endpoint and gets a new access token plus RT2. RT1 is now used.
steps.body: The app posts `grant_type=refresh_token` with RT1 to the token endpoint. The server finds RT1 **active**, marks it **used**, and returns a new access token together with a *new* refresh token, RT2, in the same family: every refresh token works exactly once. The app replaces both tokens and calls the API again.

steps.title: Reuse is detected
steps.caption: An attacker replays a stolen copy of RT1. Already used: the server revokes the whole family.
steps.body: An attacker who copied RT1 earlier now replays it. The server sees a refresh token that was already used: the sign that two parties hold tokens from this family, and it cannot tell which of them is the thief. So it revokes the **whole family**, RT2 included, and answers `invalid_grant`.

steps.title: Sign in again
steps.caption: RT2 was revoked too, so the app gets invalid_grant. The user signs in again: a new family starts.
steps.body: When its access token expires, the app sends RT2 and gets `invalid_grant` as well, so it drops its tokens and sends the user through sign-in again, which starts a new family with a new RT1. The theft has cost the user one extra sign-in. The damage is bounded: the thief has no working refresh token and holds, at most, an access token that expires within minutes.
